opening_mood.text: The Morning Brew: Squeezes, Spreads, and Stale Valuations

Happy Monday. If you spent the weekend dodging July downpours or nursing a hangover from across the pond, the markets didn't wait for you. We have a massive week ahead with the FOMC minutes and the start of Q2 earnings season, but the plumbing of the City is already shifting. From a historic index inclusion to a private equity raid on a British budget carrier, grab a coffee—or a pint, depending on how your morning is going—and let's get into what actually matters today.

content.text: The Morning Briefing: Bad News, Rocket Squeezes, and Private Equity Airline Food
The last 48 hours have delivered some of the most fascinating structural shifts we've seen all summer. Here is the breakdown of the news driving conversations across City desks today.
1. The 57k Jobs Miss: Bad News is Good News Again

On Thursday, July 2 (ahead of the Friday holiday), the US Bureau of Labor Statistics dropped a damp squib of a jobs report. The US economy added just 57,000 non-farm payrolls in June, roughly half of the 114,000 consensus estimate and the lowest print in four months. The labour market is cooling, and it's cooling fast.

This has completely flipped the script on monetary policy. The market has shifted from fearing further rate hikes to a comfortable 'wait-and-see' stance, with any hawkish July Fed moves effectively priced out. In the upside-down world of macro trading, bad economic data is the ultimate equity fuel because it keeps the Fed in its cage. Equity markets threw a party: the Dow Jones Industrial Average hit a fresh all-time high of 52,900.07 on Thursday, while the S&P 500 added 1.8%.

What to say at work: 'Bad news is officially good news again. The 57k payroll print has taken the wind right out of the hawkish sails, sending the Dow to a record high. But we have to ask: is this the perfect soft landing, or are we starting to slide into a genuine labour market contraction?'
2. SpaceX Joins the Nasdaq-100: The Ultimate Passive Squeeze

SpaceX (SPCX) is officially set to join the Nasdaq-100 index before the opening bell on Tuesday, July 7. This follows its monster ~$1.77 trillion IPO on June 12. Nasdaq utilised its newly minted 'fast-track' framework to admit Elon Musk's giant after just 15 trading days.

Trillions of dollars in passive funds tracking the Nasdaq-100 (including the $490 billion Invesco QQQ) are legally mandated to buy SpaceX shares. The catch? SpaceX only floated 4.24% of its total shares at IPO, leaving a tiny $89 billion free float. This creates a massive mechanical supply-demand mismatch. Passive trackers are forced to buy up to $27 billion in shares from an incredibly tight pool of liquidity, meaning they will have to trim holdings in other tech heavyweights to fund it.

What to say at work: 'SpaceX joining the Nasdaq-100 is the ultimate passive-flow squeeze. With a tiny 4.2% float but a massive valuation, index trackers are forced to buy into a very tight market. Watch for passive funds having to dump other tech giants to make room—it's a mechanical rebalancing that will trigger some serious volatility.'
3. EasyJet Says Yes: Castlelake's £5.5bn Take-Private Deal

Over the weekend, the board of EasyJet agreed in principle to a £5.5 billion ($7.34 billion) takeover offer from US investment firm Castlelake. The cash offer of £6.90 per share represents a 24% premium to Friday's close of £5.58 and is Castlelake's fifth attempt to buy the airline. EasyJet shares jumped over 10% in early London trading on Monday.

To bypass strict EU ownership rules (which mandate that airlines operating in the bloc must be majority-owned by EU nationals), Castlelake is partnering with Brookfield and Irish industry veterans Peter Bellew and Mark Breen, who will hold a 51% stake. It shows the sheer volume of private equity dry powder targeting unloved UK PLC.

What to say at work: 'Castlelake finally wore down EasyJet's board on their fifth try at £6.90 a share. It's a classic PE play on unloved UK equities. The clever part is the structure—using Irish co-investors to hold 51% to dodge the EU's majority-ownership rules. Expect arbitrageurs to pile in before the August 3 deadline.'
4. Meta Compute: Is the AI CapEx Boom Cracking?

Bloomberg reported that Meta Platforms is planning to launch a cloud infrastructure business, internally dubbed 'Meta Compute,' to rent out its excess AI compute capacity and host models, putting it in direct competition with AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. While Meta shares jumped on the prospect of ROI-generation, the news triggered a sharp sell-off in semiconductor and 'neocloud' stocks mid-week.

This is a massive narrative shift. If Meta has 'excess' compute capacity, it suggests the hyperscalers may have overinvested in data centres, signalling the transition from a chip shortage to a capacity glut. If a price war breaks out in rented GPU cycles, the margins for the entire AI hardware stack are in serious trouble.

What to say at work: 'Meta renting out excess AI compute is a huge warning sign for the CapEx boom. It suggests we're moving from a chip shortage to a capacity glut. If hyperscalers start price-warring each other on cloud compute, the eye-watering margins that chipmakers and neoclouds have enjoyed are going to get crushed.'
5. SCOTUS Blocks Trump's Fed Firing: Central Bank Independence Preserved

In a landmark 5-4 decision on June 29, the US Supreme Court ruled that President Trump lacked the constitutional authority to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook without cause, allowing her to remain on the board while her lawsuit proceeds. Trump attempted to fire Cook in August 2025 over unproven mortgage fraud allegations, marking the first time a president has tried to fire a Fed Governor in the central bank's 113-year history.

This is a massive relief for macro funds and rates desks. A president being able to fire Fed governors at will would have destroyed the institutional independence of the central bank, leading to a massive political risk premium being priced into US Treasuries and a potential de-anchoring of long-term inflation expectations.

What to say at work: 'The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling to block Lisa Cook's firing is a massive win for central bank independence. If Trump had won, rates desks would have had to price a permanent political risk premium into US Treasuries. The Fed's independence is the only thing keeping long-term inflation expectations anchored.'
6. ING's Wealth Play: Buying 40% of Spain's Singular Bank

Dutch lender ING announced a strategic investment to acquire a ~40% stake in leading Spanish wealth manager Singular Bank from private equity firm Warburg Pincus. Singular Bank manages around €19 billion in client assets. As net interest margins (NIM) peak and lending growth slows, European banks are desperate to expand their capital-light, fee-generating wealth management businesses.

What to say at work: 'ING taking a 40% stake in Spain's Singular Bank is a textbook capital-light growth play. With net interest margins peaking, banks are desperate for fee income that doesn't bloat their risk-weighted assets. It's a smart way to buy distribution without tying up precious CET1 capital.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Morning After: A Very Peculiar Independence Day

US markets are shaking off the long Independence Day weekend, but the silence of Friday’s holiday has only amplified the noise from Thursday’s pre-holiday session. We are looking at a market undergoing a massive structural shift. On one hand, the economy is cooling faster than a pint left out in the January rain. On the other, the long-dominant AI trade is showing its first major structural cracks, while the largest IPO in history is about to trigger a mechanical buying tsunami.
The 57k Payroll Mirage

Let’s start with the macro. Thursday’s June jobs report was a shocker, printing at just 57,000 nonfarm payrolls—well below the 115,000 consensus and the weakest showing since early 2024. To make matters worse, April and May’s numbers were quietly revised downward by a combined 74,000. On paper, the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.2%, which sounds like a win. But look under the hood: it fell because people are dropping out of the labour force entirely, with the participation rate sliding 0.3% to 61.5%.

For the City, this is a classic 'bad news is good news' setup. A rapidly cooling labour market takes the wind out of the Fed’s hawkish sails, giving policymakers plenty of cover to delay rate hikes or even bring cuts back onto the table. But there is a limit to this logic. If the consumer is tapped out and hiring is freezing up, the 'soft landing' narrative starts looking more like a controlled crash. The cross-asset read was immediate: US Treasury yields drifted lower, and capital began rotating aggressively out of cyclical growth and into defensive value.
Meta’s Gain is the Chipmakers’ Pain

The real drama, however, is in tech. While the Dow Jones surged 1.1% to a record high of 52,900 on Thursday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 0.8%. The culprit? A violent 10% to 14% two-day breakdown in the semiconductor and AI infrastructure complex.

The trigger was a Bloomberg report that Meta Platforms is planning a new public cloud service, internally dubbed 'Meta Compute'. Meta has been spending like a drunken sailor on shore leave—with 2026 capex projected at a staggering $125 billion to $145 billion. But the report revealed that Meta is looking to rent out its excess AI compute capacity and GPU cycles to third parties. This is a massive psychological shift for the market. It’s the first time a major hyperscaler has admitted to having surplus capacity. If Meta has spare GPUs lying around, the narrative of an infinite, insatiable demand for AI chips is dead. The 'neocloud' players like CoreWeave (which Meta previously rented space from) fell over 10% on the threat of direct competition, while semiconductor heavyweights like SanDisk (-14%) and KLA Corp (-11.5%) were absolutely battered.
The SpaceX Forced-Buying Tsunami

If you think the tech volatility is over, brace yourselves for tonight. Today, Monday, July 6, marks the 15th trading session for Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX) since its historic $2 trillion IPO on June 12. Under the Nasdaq’s newly minted 'fast-entry' rules—widely seen as a bespoke red carpet rolled out to court Elon Musk—SpaceX is set to join the Nasdaq-100 index before the market opens tomorrow, July 7.

This is where the plumbing of passive investing gets incredibly messy. Trillions of dollars in passive capital track the Nasdaq-100 (Invesco’s QQQ alone manages over $480 billion). Tonight, after the closing bell, every single one of these index funds is legally mandated to buy SpaceX shares to match the new index weight. J.P. Morgan estimates this will trigger between $4.3 billion and $7 billion in forced passive inflows.

The catch? SpaceX’s public float is a tiny 3% to 5% of its total shares. You have billions of dollars of non-discretionary, price-insensitive capital chasing a microscopic sliver of tradeable stock. It is a textbook supply-demand squeeze. Active managers have been front-running this all week, but the actual mechanical rebalance happens tonight. If you want to see how index construction rules can distort asset prices, grab a pint and watch the SPCX ticker at the close.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is watching from the sidelines. S&P Dow Jones Indices refused to bend their rules, maintaining that SpaceX must show 12 months of trading history and GAAP profitability (SpaceX lost $4.94 billion in 2025) before getting in. This sets up a fascinating divergence: Nasdaq-100 trackers are forced to buy a highly volatile, low-float rocket ship today, while S&P 500 trackers are safely insulated. It’s a great talking point for your next client meeting: when does passive investing stop being a passive reflection of the market and start becoming a forced driver of it?

sections.title: Financial Idea: Why EV/EBITDA is Structurally Broken for Banks

content.text: The Concept: Debt is Raw Material, Cash is Inventory

If you want to instantly out yourself as a novice in an investment meeting or an interview, try pitching a bank using EV/EBITDA. It is the financial equivalent of trying to order a pint of Guinness in a boutique vegan tea room—it shows a fundamental misunderstanding of where you are. For non-financial companies, EV/EBITDA is the undisputed workhorse of valuation. But for banks, insurers, and other financial institutions, both halves of the ratio are completely broken.

To understand why, we have to look at how a bank actually works. For a normal company—say, a widget manufacturer—debt is a capital structure choice. They can fund their factories with equity or debt. Cash is just idle fuel sitting in the tank. This is why we calculate Enterprise Value (EV) as Equity Value + Net Debt. We want to isolate the value of the core operating assets, regardless of how they are funded.

But for a bank, this logic completely collapses. First, debt (deposits) is the raw material. When you deposit £1,000 into your Barclays account, that deposit is technically a liability (debt) on Barclays' balance sheet. But Barclays does not treat it as 'financing' in the traditional sense. It is the raw material they use to package up and sell as loans. Second, cash is the inventory. A bank's cash isn't 'idle'. It is the very product they trade in. They need massive cash reserves to meet regulatory requirements and fund daily withdrawals.

If you blindly apply the standard EV formula (Equity + Debt - Cash) to a bank, you end up adding its massive deposit base as debt and subtracting its cash. Because banks are highly leveraged by design (often 10:1 or more), you get a massive, volatile EV that tells you absolutely nothing about the business's actual operating value. In fact, during market panics, some banks have ended up with negative enterprise values on paper—which is a mathematical quirk of having massive cash balances relative to a depressed market cap, not a screaming buy signal.
The EBITDA Problem: Ignoring the Cost of Flour

The denominator is even worse. EBITDA stands for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation. We add back interest expense because we want to see operating profitability before financing costs.

For a bank, interest expense is not a financing cost. It is their single largest operating cost—the interest they pay to depositors and wholesale lenders. Stripping out interest expense to calculate a bank's 'EBITDA' is like calculating a bakery's profitability while ignoring the cost of flour. It is completely meaningless. A bank's core business is the spread between what it earns on loans (interest income) and what it pays on deposits (interest expense). If you ignore the interest expense, you ignore the business.
A Simple Numerical Example
Let’s look at a hypothetical bank, 'Thames & Trent PLC':

items: Market Cap: £5 billion
Total Deposits (Debt): £45 billion
Cash & Reserves: £5 billion
Interest Income: £2.0 billion
Interest Expense: £1.2 billion
Non-Interest Operating Costs: £300 million

content.text: If you tried to calculate EV, you would get £5bn (Equity) + £45bn (Debt) - £5bn (Cash) = £45 billion. If Thames & Trent suddenly attracts £5bn more in deposits, its 'debt' goes up, and its EV magically jumps to £50 billion, making it look 'more expensive' on an EV basis, even though its business just grew.

Now look at the income statement. Net Interest Income is £800m (£2.0bn - £1.2bn). After subtracting £300m of operating costs, the bank's pre-tax operating profit is £500m. If you calculate 'EBITDA' by adding back the £1.2bn interest expense, you get £1.7bn. But that £1.2bn is a real, cash operating cost! You cannot run the bank without paying your depositors.
What to Use Instead

Because you cannot cleanly separate 'operating' and 'financing' activities for a financial institution, you must value them using equity-side metrics. The capital structure is the business. Therefore, we use:

items: Price-to-Earnings (P/E): Since net income is 'post-interest', it correctly captures the net interest margin (the spread).

Price-to-Book (P/B) or Price-to-Tangible Book (P/TBV): Banks are essentially piles of financial assets and liabilities. The book value of their equity is a highly relevant anchor for valuation, especially when compared to their Return on Equity (ROE).

content.text: How to Use This in Interviews and at Work

This is a classic 'filter' question in investment banking (especially FIG teams) and asset management interviews. If asked how to value a bank, you should immediately steer away from EV and standard DCF (unless it's a Dividend Discount Model or Residual Income Model) and focus on P/E, P/TBV, and the ROE-to-Cost of Equity relationship.

If you're chatting with colleagues or a client over a pint, you can sum it up like this: 'Trying to use EV/EBITDA on a bank is like trying to measure a runner's speed by looking at their shoe size. It is the wrong metric for the wrong asset class. For banks, debt isn't leverage; it's the inventory. If you ignore the interest paid on deposits, you're ignoring the cost of goods sold.'

content.text: The Finance-Informed Neural Network (FINN)

We’ve all seen machine learning models try to price options. Usually, they do one of two things: either they blindly fit historical option prices (and end up violating basic no-arbitrage rules, producing 'Greeks' that look like a random walk), or they use Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to solve the Black-Scholes PDE. But PINNs are a pain—they require you to write down the exact PDE, which gets incredibly messy if you have stochastic volatility, jumps, or high-dimensional baskets. Enter the Finance-Informed Neural Network (FINN), a framework that skips the PDE entirely and learns to price options the way a real trading desk does: through dynamic replication.

The core idea is beautifully simple. Instead of training the network on option prices, you train it on a self-supervised replication-consistency objective. You set up a neural network to predict the option price g(t, S_t). Because it’s a neural network, you can use automatic differentiation to get the exact Delta (the derivative of price with respect to spot) and Gamma at any point. You then simulate stock price paths and run a virtual delta-hedging portfolio. At each step, you update the portfolio's wealth using the network's Delta. At maturity, the portfolio's final value should perfectly match the option's payoff (like a standard call option payoff). The loss function is simply the squared difference between the final portfolio value and the payoff. If the network minimises this replication error, the law of one price guarantees that the network's output is the unique, arbitrage-free option price.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class FINN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # Inputs: time-to-maturity (tau), spot price (S)
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 64),
            nn.Softplus(), # Softplus ensures smooth, continuous Greeks
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.Softplus(),
            nn.Linear(64, 1)
        )
    def forward(self, tau, S):
        return self.net(torch.cat([tau, S], dim=-1))

# Inside the training loop:
# S is the stock price path of shape (steps, batch_size, 1)
# V is the hedging portfolio value, initialized to the model's predicted price at t=0
V = model(tau[0], S[0])
for t in range(num_steps - 1):
    # Compute Delta using PyTorch autograd
    S_t = S[t].clone().requires_grad_(True)
    price = model(tau[t], S_t)
    delta = torch.autograd.grad(price.sum(), S_t, create_graph=True)[0]
    
    # Update self-financing portfolio: stock holdings + risk-free cash
    dS = S[t+1] - S_t
    cash = V - delta * S_t
    V = delta * S[t+1] + cash * torch.exp(r * dt)

# Loss is the replication error at maturity T
payoff = torch.clamp(S[-1] - strike, min=0.0)
loss = torch.mean((V - payoff) ** 2)

This approach comes from a paper by Amine M. Aboussalah and co-authors, 'Finance-Informed Neural Network: Learning the Geometry of Option Pricing' (revised in March 2026). The beauty of FINN is that fundamental pricing relationships, like put-call parity, emerge endogenously without being hardcoded. Even better, because it only needs spot price paths to train, you can use it to construct coherent option prices and Greeks for illiquid assets that don't even have a listed options market. You just train the model on historical spot data, and it learns the implied pricing operator.

If you want to sound like the smartest person in the pub (or your next interview), this is your golden ticket. When someone brings up 'Deep Hedging', point out that Deep Hedging is utility-centric—it finds the optimal hedge for a specific risk-averse agent. FINN, on the other hand, is operator-centric—it uses the replication objective to back out the actual arbitrage-free pricing function itself. It’s the ultimate bridge between pure data-driven ML and classical mathematical finance.

Of course, there's a catch. Like any model-free method, FINN is highly sensitive to the quality of your spot price simulator or historical paths. If your simulator doesn't capture real-world fat tails or regime shifts, your replicated prices will be miles off. Furthermore, in the real world, transaction costs and discrete hedging intervals mean perfect replication is impossible. If you don't regularise the loss for transaction costs, the network might learn highly volatile Delta strategies that look great in a frictionless simulation but would bankrupt a real trading desk in a week.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Paper: The Fragility of Semi-Liquid Private Credit

If you have spent more than five minutes in a City pub recently, you will know that private credit is the industry's current obsession. But as the asset class tries to 'democratise' itself by selling to retail investors and wealth managers, a massive structural question has emerged: how do you promise regular liquidity when your underlying assets are about as liquid as cold porridge? A brilliant NBER working paper, 'The Fragility of Semi-Liquid Private Credit Funds' (June 2026) by Chuck Fang, Itay Goldstein, and Yao Zeng, takes a sledgehammer to the industry's favourite new structure.
Why This One?

Semi-liquid private credit funds—mostly structured as perpetual Business Development Companies (BDCs) or interval funds—have exploded from $10 billion in 2019 to over $300 billion today. To keep retail investors happy, they offer quarterly redemptions, usually capped at 5% of net assets. The industry line is that this 5% gate makes them 'run-proof'. This paper is the first major academic study to look under the hood and prove that these gates do not actually eliminate run-like fragility; they just slow it down while creating some nasty game-theoretic incentives.
The Core Mechanics

items: The Liquidity Illusion: Cash buffers in these funds average only about 5% of net assets, and quarterly loan repayments bring in less than 1%. If a fund hits its 5% redemption cap for two quarters in a row, it is out of cash.
The Negative Co-movement: Inflows dry up precisely when outflows spike. You cannot rely on new retail money to pay off the old retail money when the market gets jittery.

The Leverage Trap: To meet redemptions without fire-selling loans, funds draw down on external credit lines (revolvers) and delay payments via 'repurchases payable'. This spikes the fund's leverage, leaving remaining investors holding a riskier, more leveraged portfolio.

Stale NAVs & First-Mover Advantage: Private loans are valued using mark-to-model estimates that lag the market. If the real value of the portfolio falls but the reported Net Asset Value (NAV) remains stale, early redeemers get out at an inflated price. The remaining investors bear the dilution.

content.text: The Game Theory: Strategic Complementarity

This is the killer point for interviews or client chats. Because early redeemers exit at inflated NAVs and leave behind a more leveraged, illiquid portfolio, a classic 'strategic complementarity' arises. In plain English: if you think other people are going to redeem next quarter, you have a massive incentive to get your redemption request in first. The 5% gate does not stop the run; it just turns it into a slow-motion queue where everyone is trying to push to the front.

Overall, our evidence suggests that quarterly gates and redemption caps do not eliminate run-like fragility in semi-liquid private credit funds, raising cautions about expanding retail access to private credit markets.
The Industry Strikes Back

Naturally, the private credit lobby is not taking this lying down. Cliffwater, a major private debt specialist, immediately fired back with a critique, calling the paper 'flawed both in content and interpretation'. They point out that perpetual BDC leverage was actually below historical peaks in early 2026, which runs counter to the paper's doom-loop narrative. They argue that committed credit facilities and the 5% cap are highly effective liability management tools designed precisely to handle these cycles without systemic distress.
How to Use This at Work (or Over a Pint)

items: In an Interview: If you are interviewing in asset management or private markets, do not just say 'private credit is growing'. Bring this up. Explain how the 'retailisation' of private markets is hitting a liquidity mismatch wall, and mention the game theory of 'strategic complementarity' in semi-liquid BDCs.
With Colleagues: Ask them: 'Are we pricing the liquidity transformation risk in these evergreen structures properly, or are we just relying on the 5% gate to save us?'

Over a Pint: Frame it as the classic finance paradox: Wall Street always tries to turn illiquid, high-yield assets into liquid, retail-friendly products, and it always ends with someone getting gated.

content.text: What to Skim

Skip the heavy econometric regressions in the middle of the paper where they prove the negative co-movement of flows. Focus on Section 1 (the introduction), Section 4 (where they break down the liquidity sources against the 5% cap), and the conclusion. That is where the commercial meat is.

sections.title: People & Psychology: The Illusion of Explanatory Depth

content.text: The Illusion of Explanatory Depth: Why Everyone is Bluffing (And How to Use It)

Picture this: You’re in a meeting room in Moorgate, and a colleague is holding court. They are talking about 'multi-agent AI workflows', 'risk-parity portfolios', or 'tokenised real-world assets' with the casual confidence of a surgeon. They sound brilliant. The client is nodding. You’re starting to feel a mild wave of imposter syndrome.

But here is a comforting, scientifically proven truth: there is a very high chance they have absolutely no idea what they are talking about. And if you asked them to explain the actual mechanics, they would fall apart faster than a cheap umbrella in a London drizzle.
The Science: Zippers, Toilets, and False Confidence

In 2002, Yale cognitive scientists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil identified this phenomenon and named it the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED). They asked participants to rate how well they understood everyday objects like zippers, flush toilets, and cylinder locks. Naturally, people gave themselves high scores. We use zippers and toilets every day; of course we know how they work.

Then, the researchers asked them to do something deceptively simple: write down a detailed, step-by-step explanation of exactly how those objects operate. The results were hilarious. Participants immediately ran out of words. They realised they didn't actually know how the teeth of a zipper mesh, or how a toilet's siphon works. When asked to re-rate their understanding after this exercise, their self-assessed scores plummeted. They had mistaken familiarity for comprehension.
Why the City is an IOED Hotspot

In finance and tech, we don't deal with zippers; we deal with highly abstract, complex systems. Because we use the terminology daily, we assume we understand the plumbing. This leads to classic corporate scenarios:

items: The Client: 'We want to deploy a generative AI agent to completely automate our credit risk assessment.' (But they can't explain how they will prevent the LLM from hallucinating synthetic financial data.)
The Pitch: 'Our proprietary multi-factor model dynamically rotates sectors to capture alpha in all market regimes.' (But the presenter can't explain the mathematical trigger for the rotation.)
The Candidate: 'Yes, I’m highly familiar with how Transformer models work.' (But they freeze when asked to sketch the self-attention mechanism on a whiteboard.)

content.text: How to Use This to Your Advantage
Once you understand that most people are suffering from IOED, you can use it as a superpower in three distinct ways:

items: 1. The 'Explain the Plumbing' Meeting Hack: When a colleague or client is aggressively pushing a half-baked, buzzword-heavy strategy, do not argue with them. Arguing makes people defensive and dig in. Instead, politely ask them to explain the mechanics. Say: 'That sounds like a great angle. Just so I can picture it, could you walk me through the step-by-step mechanics of how the model decides to rotate out of tech?' They will hit the boundaries of their own knowledge, realise they are bluffing, and naturally moderate their stance. You win the point without ever having to say 'you're wrong.'

2. The Interview Shield: Assume your interviewer knows about IOED. If you put 'Machine Learning', 'LBO modelling', or 'Python' on your CV, expect them to hand you a marker and say, 'Great, draw the mechanics on the board.' If you can't explain the plumbing, don't put it on your CV.

3. The Self-Check: Before you pitch a new idea to your boss or investment committee, force yourself to write down a step-by-step explanation of how it works on a single sheet of paper. If you find yourself writing 'and then a miracle happens,' you've got IOED. Fix it before they find out.

content.text: One Line to Remember
If you can't explain the plumbing, don't try to sell the palace.
